La solución a los tres agujeros es la mi: The solution to all three holes is the same: before being raised to $e$, the message is padded with randomness up to the size of $n$ with a fixed scheme. The current standard, OAEP, mixes the message with random bytes through a hash function, so that the same message gives different ciphertexts every time, multiplying ciphertexts produces rubbish on decryption, and there is never a small $m$. The old padding, PKCS#1 v1.5, had a famous flaw that will be seen in the topic on side channels.
Lo anterior es el RSA que se explica, y: The above is the RSA that gets explained, and it has three holes that have nothing to do with factoring. First, it is deterministic: the same message always gives the same ciphertext, so if the message is “yes” or “no”, Eve encrypts both with the public key and compares. Second, it is malleable: ciphertexts multiply.
Los bits de RSA no se comparan directame: RSA's bits do not compare directly with AES's, because the attack is not brute force but factoring, which grows more slowly than $2^{\text{bits}}$. That is why 3072 bits of RSA are needed to match 128 of AES, and 15,360 to match 256. That disproportion is the reason elliptic curves, with 256 bits, have been replacing RSA.

RSA de libro es determinista, multiplica: Textbook RSA is deterministic, multiplicative and vulnerable with a small $e$: that is why the message is padded with randomness (OAEP) before encrypting.
RSA es el sistema de clave pública más f: RSA is the most famous public-key system and the one longest in use. The mathematics fits in three lines; the complete system, the one that withstands Eve, has a few more, and each one is there because of an attack that worked.
RSA firma los certificados de la mayoría: RSA signs the certificates of most websites, the software packages of operating systems and electronic documents; it encrypts email with PGP and the session keys of many old protocols. Chip payment cards carry a 1024- or 2048-bit RSA that signs every transaction. And the electronic identity card holds two RSA key pairs: one to identify yourself and another to sign.
Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir y Leonard Adleman: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman published it in 1977; as Rivest tells it, the idea came to him one April night after a Passover dinner. Martin Gardner made it public in August in Scientific American with a challenge: a message encrypted with a 129-digit $n$, RSA-129, which was decrypted in 1994 by six hundred volunteers over the internet: it said “the magic words are squeamish ossifrage”. In 1997 it became known that Clifford Cocks, of the British intelligence service, had invented the same thing in 1973 and had left it in a drawer. The RSA patent expired in the year 2000.
